doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Listening: sound as personality, Higgins, Blakey and Cannonball
summary: After an audio clip, Harper says a drummer's sound is his personality, with stories of Blakey playing cases and Higgins using a phone book.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. I wrote one on there.
What is it about that, for you, that is just so — it gets you in the heart?

That song, it swings. And like I said, for me I guess when I think about a lot of those guys in that era, you know, the intent that they played with, for me, you can feel all that. You can’t get away from it. Higgins, Art Blakey. I’d say we were tight. Because I loved his sound. And the way he played was his personality.
You know some people would go oh wait a minute, what do you mean you love his sound? Like how can you tell one drummer from another?

Well especially in that period with a lot of the great players, it’s just like when you would talk to some people that might be into let’s say metaphysics and spiritual things, when they talk about everybody has an aura you know. A guy’s sound is like his aura. Just like when you were talking about Cannonball. It was his personality. And it comes through the horns. And still with a lot of players you can see that their personalities would transcend and come through the instrument. Some of the inner things that you don’t see unless you know them well, all of that will tend to come out. Like you might have some guys that you think are just quiet, they don’t say a whole lot. But then when they play you say wow, that’s kind of surprising. But if you got to know them you’d know that that’s coming out of what is inside. So that’s a lot of what their sound and their personality is.
Does it have also, the way they tune their drums or, sort of the gear thing?

There’s some aspects of that. There’s some of it. But it’s not totally. Because I mean I’ve spent so much time going to see Higgins and let him use my drums, you know what I mean? Or Art Blakey. Or hearing those stories about Art Blakey getting to the gig, they were on tour somewhere in Europe and there was no drums you know what I mean. But there were some cases over in the corner so he pulled out the cases and played the cases. You know what I mean? You know, and those guys, through their personalities still make

the music work. I remember Higgins telling me stories about that period when he was, you know, life was really a struggle for him. He had pawned his drums and he’d come to the gig and no drums. And he’d go in the back of the Vanguard and come out with a phone book and a coat hanger or something, and still make a gig. You’d hear about guys playing a pie pan, and they could still — you know their sound is there.

You know Carl Allen told this anecdote about Billy Higgins. He was playing in a club and he says that he was just sort of not really doing it. And all of a sudden this hand came over and took over on the ride cymbal and it was Billy Higgins. And he said the whole room just like —
That’s amazing that a person could have that kind of force without bashing.

Right. Because I mean, like I said, it’s that inside, that intent, where you know how to give what you need, and so much spiritual energy is coming out through you, that you are able to bring up and call forth. But I mean if anybody knew Cannonball you’d hear some of the same stories about Cannonball. People tell me man, Cannon’s personality, even when he wasn’t playing, if he walked in the room it was just something about him, you just knew Cannon was there. Well that’s the same way with his sound. So a lot of guys are like that. You know, Art Blakey, Elvin [Jones] and guys, I mean Billy Taylor. He’s another one. When you’ve heard him play, his sound fit his personality. Genuine, no frills, just down to earth, the right thing.
